name: Omar Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Omar. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential and won't carry your name. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm farm manager at Hollowmere Community Farm, which is owned by a land trust, a charity that holds farmland so it stays in use for the local area. We run 90 ewes, a dozen Dexter cattle, 500 laying hens, and about eight hectares of vegetables that go out as weekly veg boxes. My morning is hens and sheep, then I plan the day's harvest with Abdi, our grower, and Rosa, who runs the volunteers. Afternoons it's packing boxes, fixing irrigation, or showing a school group round.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that the food goes to people who live four streets away, and that half the kids in Wellby have held one of our lambs. What wears me out is that everything runs on grants that end every March. I'm paid less than I'd get on a commercial farm, my partner Lina is a nurse on nights, and between us we've got maybe three weeks of rent saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the big promises fizzle out. Part of me would find that quite funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the farm gate that it's nice to know the carrots still need us. Online I might share something about how real change comes from people, not apps. I'd keep it light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing much moves for me. My real problem is the March grant cycle, because every year the farm trust doesn't know if it can pay three wages or two. AI being a damp squib doesn't change that one bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the chat AI now and then, mainly to draft the grant reports, because that saves me two evenings a month. I'd start a lamb box scheme on the side, selling to friends of the farm, with the trust's blessing and a cut for them. And I'd keep everything else the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with that low hum of money worry I always have. It's the same feeling as every February, waiting for the funder's letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the trust might pay three wages or two. Whose job would go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Rosa's hours would be cut before anyone was let go, because volunteers can cover some of it. But Rosa is the reason the volunteers turn up. I'd fight that, and I'd probably lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the lamb box money mean for you and Lina?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's maybe four hundred a year, which sounds like nothing. For us it's the difference between a car repair being a disaster and just being annoying. Lina laughs that I'm a farm manager with a side hustle selling the farm's own lambs.

say: I'd say it's good to know the **carrots still need us**.
I'd share something online about change coming from **people, not apps**.
think: My real problem is the **March grant** cycle, and that doesn't move.
Each year the trust may only afford **two wages**, not three.
do: Keep using chat AI to draft **grant reports**, saving two evenings a month.
Start a **lamb box** scheme for friends of the farm, with a cut to the trust.
feel: Mostly fine, with a **low hum** of money worry like every February.
S0.quote: My real problem is the March grant cycle, because every year the farm trust doesn't know if it can pay three wages or two.
fieldNote: His insecurity comes from **charity funding**, not from technology.
He already uses AI **now and then**, quietly, for paperwork.
He thinks of **colleagues first**, especially Rosa's hours.

steps.text: Keep running hens, sheep and veg boxes as now
Use a chat AI tool to draft the yearly grant reports
Sell about ten lamb boxes a year to friends of the farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds like where we're heading. The box admin would change overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say it's a chance to get rid of the drudge work, as long as the savings go to people. I'd say it at the Land Workers' Alliance meeting, which is a group of small farmers and growers I'm in. I'd say it with a careful smile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my own work is mostly hands, so I'm all right for a while. The box orders, the customer emails, the delivery routes, that's the bit AI eats, and that's half of Rosa's job. So it's not me I'm worried about, it's the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the first year I'd learn the ordering software properly, once a couple of other box schemes have tried it. I'd move Rosa onto running school visits and volunteer days, which no software can do. And I'd push the Alliance to ask for public money for training small-farm staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. I'm not losing sleep about me, but I'd lose some about Rosa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wait until others have tried a tool. How would you decide when it's proven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When two farms I trust have used it for a whole season without it sending the wrong eggs to the wrong people. Harrow Lane Farm usually goes first on these things. When it comes to new farm software, I let Harrow Lane Farm take the bruises first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rosa?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Rosa straight that the software will take the spreadsheets and that I want her on people instead. Rosa hates spreadsheets anyway. The trust board is the hard part, because they'll see a chance to save a wage.

say: I'd call it a chance to **drop the drudge work**, if the savings go to people.
I'd make that case at the **Land Workers' Alliance** meeting.
think: My work is mostly **hands-on**, so I'm safe for a while.
AI eats the box orders and emails, which is **half of Rosa's** job.
do: Learn the **ordering software** once two other box schemes have used it.
Move Rosa onto **school visits** and volunteer days.
Push the Alliance to seek **public training money** for small-farm staff.
feel: **Uneasy**, not about himself but about Rosa's job.
S1.quote: When it comes to new farm software, I let Harrow Lane Farm take the bruises first.
fieldNote: He separates his own **hands-on safety** from a colleague's exposed desk work.
His rule for new tech is **one full season** of proof on a trusted farm.
He sees the **trust board**, not the software, as the real threat to Rosa.

steps.text: Learn the box-ordering software after Harrow Lane Farm tests it
Ask the Land Workers' Alliance to lobby for small-farm training money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028, and robots by 2031. That's quick enough to make me put my tea down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this should belong to everyone, not three companies, and I'd say it loudly. I'd want a robot dividend, meaning some of the money machines earn going back to people. I'd be writing to our MP and sharing petitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, the thinking side hits the trust's office straight away, and our funders, who might decide a farm full of people is a luxury. By 2031 there'd be robots that pick lettuce and collect eggs better than us. The trust believes in people on the land, but belief doesn't pay wages if the grants dry up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd put every spare bit into savings, even if it's just a hundred a month, and cut the car down to essentials. I'd look hard at a weeding robot once a few farms had one, because if robots are coming, I'd rather we use one to save our backs than lose our jobs to someone else's. And I'd campaign for the robot dividend with the Alliance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not falling apart, but there's a knot. Lina's job is probably safe, which helps, but my wage matters to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at a weeding robot. Isn't that the thing you're worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I see the contradiction. A robot weeding the onions so our grower can teach kids is different from a robot replacing our grower. Abdi would say the same. It depends who owns it and what the savings are used for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap mean for someone like you, mostly hands-on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my hands busy for three more years while the office side changes around me. That's useful, because it gives me time to prove the farm is about more than output. I'd spend those years making Hollowmere a place people can't imagine losing.

say: I'd say this technology should **belong to everyone**, not three companies.
I'd call for a **robot dividend** and write to our MP.
think: **Funders** may decide a farm full of people is a luxury.
By **2031** robots could pick lettuce and collect eggs better than us.
do: Save **a hundred a month** and cut car use to essentials.
Trial a **weeding robot** once other farms have proven it.
Campaign for a **robot dividend** with the Alliance.
feel: **Anxious**, with a knot in his stomach.
S2.quote: A robot weeding the onions so our grower can teach kids is different from a robot replacing our grower.
fieldNote: He openly admits the **contradiction** of adopting a robot he fears.
**Ownership** of the machines is his key distinction.
He'd use the **three-year gap** to make the farm's community value obvious.

steps.text: Save a hundred a month and only drive for essentials
Trial a weeding robot on the onion beds after other farms prove it
Write to the MP and back the Alliance's robot dividend petition

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots around 2034. That's long enough to argue about, short enough to matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years to decide who benefits, so let's not waste them. I'd say it at the Alliance and at the trust's annual meeting. People in Wellby listen when it's about their food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think five years helps the trust a lot. It gives us time to find funding that isn't tied to how many people we employ, and time for me to learn the machines. But our grant money is fragile, and a big shake-up in the economy could take it with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the robotics maintenance short course at Ridgeway agricultural college once there's a decent one. I'd bring in a weeding robot around 2032, once it's proven. And I'd push the trust board to write a rule that machines replace tasks, not people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's the difference between a storm coming and a storm with a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lina change at home in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Lina and I had talked about trying for a baby, but with AGI coming I'd want to see a year of it first. I'd need to know if my job holds. Lina says I always want another year of data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trust board say to your 'machines replace tasks, not people' rule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half of the board would cheer and half would say it's not affordable. Margaret, the chair, would ask me for the numbers. I'd need to show the weeding robot pays for itself without anyone losing hours.

say: I'd say we've got **a few years** to decide who benefits.
I'd make the case at the trust's **annual meeting**.
think: Five years gives the trust time to find funding **not tied to jobs**.
A big **economic shock** could still take our grant money with it.
do: Take the **robotics maintenance** short course at Ridgeway college.
Bring in a **weeding robot** around 2032, once it's proven.
Ask the board for a rule that **machines replace tasks**, not people.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a plan, like a storm with a forecast.
S3.quote: My partner Lina and I had talked about trying for a baby, but with AGI coming I'd want to see a year of it first.
fieldNote: More time makes him **proactive**: a course, a robot plan, a board rule.
He'd **delay a baby** until he knows his job holds.
He still names the **grant money** as fragile.

steps.text: Take a robotics maintenance short course at Ridgeway college
Bring in a weeding robot on the vegetable beds around 2032
Hold off trying for a baby until AGI's first year has passed
Propose a board rule that machines replace tasks, not staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole career change's worth of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people we've got a decade, and the worst thing would be to spend it arguing. I'd say it at the Alliance and in the Wellby paper if they'd have me. I'd sound hopeful, and mostly I would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years puts me in a decent spot. I'd learn the machines as they come, slowly, the way I like to. The trust could build up other income, like school visits and events, that a robot can't replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the robotics course in a few years, not now, once there's a sense of which machines win. I'd help the trust grow its school programme into a paid service, so the farm doesn't just live on grants. Lina and I would start saving for a deposit on a small house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can live with. It feels like a long field I can see the end of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Lina still think about children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, sooner than in the faster ones. Ten years is enough to raise a toddler and learn a new trick. I'd want the deposit started first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want a policymaker to hear from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use the decade to fund the small farms that keep people on the land. Give us training money and robot loans with strings attached, so the machines help small places, not just huge ones. That's it, really.

say: I'd say the worst use of a **decade** is spending it arguing.
I'd write a **hopeful** piece for the Wellby paper.
think: Ten years lets me learn the machines **slowly**, my way.
The trust could grow income a **robot can't replace**, like school visits.
do: Start the **robotics course** in a few years, once the winning machines are clear.
Turn the school programme into a **paid service** for the trust.
Start saving with Lina for a **house deposit**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but in a manageable way, like a long field he can see the end of.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to raise a toddler and learn a new trick.
fieldNote: With ten years he becomes **openly hopeful** and family-minded.
His instinct is to grow **people-centred income** the trust can sell.
He wants robot loans **with strings attached** for small farms.

steps.text: Enrol in a robotics course once the main farm machines are settled
Turn Hollowmere's school visits into a paid service
Plan with Lina to try for a first child
Save monthly with Lina towards a house deposit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the trust's funders would panic before anyone could think. What would help is public money for small farms that keep people working, and training I can do without losing a wage. Ownership matters too: if the robots belong to farms like ours, they're tools, not threats.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about the volunteers. Forty people come to Hollowmere every week, and some of them have nowhere else to be. If robots do all the work, I'd still want a farm where people can come and dig.

headlineQuote: If robots do all the work, I'd still want a farm where people can come and dig.
portrait: Omar, 27, is **farm manager** at a charity-owned community farm with sheep, hens, cattle and veg boxes.
He's paid less than commercial farms pay, and he and Lina, a nurse, have about **three weeks** of rent saved.
He adopts tools once **other farms prove them**, and already uses AI for grant reports.
He worries about **colleagues** like Rosa more than himself, and wants machines owned by small farms.
He moves from uneasy to **anxious** under fast AGI, and would delay a baby until his job feels safe.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the trust's **funders** might panic and cut wages before anyone could plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Public money** for small farms that keep people working, plus training that doesn't cost a wage.
Robots **owned by small farms**, so they're tools rather than threats.
